html:
The Neo-Babylonian Empire was the last empire ruled by native kings of Mesopotamia, from 626 BCE, when Nabopolassar became king of Babylon, until Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BCE. It is best known for Nebuchadnezzar II and the great city of Babylon.

Nabopolassar led Babylon in revolt against Assyria. Allied with the Medes of Iran, he sacked the Assyrian capital, Nineveh, in 612 BCE, and by 609 BCE Assyria was gone. Babylon took over most of its empire in Mesopotamia and the Levant.

His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605 to 562 BCE) beat Egypt in Syria and secured the Levant. When Judah rebelled, he took Jerusalem in 597 BCE and in 586 BCE destroyed the city and its temple, taking many of its people into exile in Babylon.

He spent the empire's wealth rebuilding Babylon:

  • Huge double walls and the blue glazed-brick Ishtar Gate, decorated with lions, bulls and dragons.
  • A great ziggurat, Etemenanki, likely the origin of the story of the Tower of Babel.
  • Palaces where later Greek writers placed the Hanging Gardens, though no Babylonian text mentions them.

Babylonian scholars kept careful records of the sky in this period, which later helped Greek astronomy.

The last king, Nabonidus, spent about ten years at an oasis in Arabia and angered Babylon's priests by favouring the moon god. In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great took Babylon, almost without a fight, and the city became part of the Persian Empire.
